samples.summary: Attacker-triggerable "unbound callback" path aborts the login and advertises the flag that disables the nonce binding
samples.evidence: The no-`state` branch is reachable by anyone who can reach the loopback listener, which is exactly the threat model the nonce exists for: a malicious page in the browser (cross-origin ``/`fetch(..., {mode:'no-cors'})` to `http://127.0.0.1:/callback?code=ATTACKER_CODE`) or any local process can send a callback with no `state` at all. login.ts:263-271 then calls `callbackReject(new Error(UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE))`, killing the in-flight login, and UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE (login.ts:216-220) asserts a cause the CLI cannot actually distinguish ("The server ... did not echo this invocation's nonce") and offers the remedy "re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback`". A user who follows the CLI's own advice re-runs with `allowUnbound: true`, at which point the identical nonce-less spray IS accepted (the `received === null` guard is skipped) and the attacker's authorization code is exchanged at `${server}/auth/cli/exchange` and written to `~/.wafflebase/session.json` as the user's session — the precise attack the nonce was added to prevent. Net: an attacker can (a) DoS every login attempt and (b) social-engineer the control off using the tool's own error text. A missing `state` should be treated like a wrong one (400, do not settle, keep waiting) with the version-skew hint deferred to the 30-second timeout, so an injected request cannot cause the abort or the downgrade advice.

samples.summary: The URL printed for headless copy-paste omits `cliState`, so the documented headless flow always produces an unbound callback and steers users to `--allow-unbound-callback`
samples.evidence: login.ts:71-76 builds `oauthUrl` with `&cliState=<nonce>` but prints `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}` — deliberately nonce-stripped — and the old "If the browser does not open, visit the URL above." line was removed; the full URL is printed only in the `catch` around `open()`. `open()` frequently resolves successfully while opening nothing (SSH sessions with a stub xdg-open, WSL, containers), and docs/design/cli.md:176 still documents step 3 as "(also prints URL for copy-paste in headless environments)". A user who copies the printed URL starts a flow with no `cliState`, so `normalizeCliState` returns undefined (github-auth.guard.ts:70), `state.cliState` is falsy at auth.controller.ts:130, and the loopback redirect carries no `state`. The CLI then aborts with UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE, which blames the server and recommends `--allow-unbound-callback` — training the ordinary headless user to run every login with the anti-injection binding disabled. The printed line should carry the full URL (or omit the copy-paste affordance entirely and say so).

samples.summary: The login nonce is sent as a query parameter, so it lands in backend/reverse-proxy access logs
samples.evidence: `GET ${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}&cliState=${nonce}` (login.ts:71-73) puts the binding secret in the request line, which every reverse proxy and Nest/Express access log records verbatim. Anyone with log or proxy visibility can read the nonce and, within the 30-second listener window, inject their own authorization code into the victim's loopback listener (the listener only checks `stateMatches`, login.ts:276). This repo already treats URL placement of access-relevant values as a hazard for the analogous case — auth.controller.ts:60-65 documents using POST with the share token in the body "so the (access-granting) token stays out of request URLs and access logs" — yet the new risk table in docs/design/rest-api.md:378-380 records only the argv exposure, not the log exposure.

samples.summary: `csrf` is minted, stored and returned by `consumeState` but never compared anywhere, while rest-api.md claims it is "validated on callback"
samples.evidence: `randomBytes(32)` is stored as `csrf` in every StateEntry and is now explicitly re-exported from the widened `consumeState` return type (cli-auth.store.ts:45-59), but a repo-wide case-insensitive grep for `csrf` finds it only in cli-auth.store.ts, its spec, and an unrelated cookie comment in auth.controller.ts:262 — no call site ever compares it. Meanwhile docs/design/rest-api.md risk table asserts "Backend generates a random 32-byte CSRF token per OAuth request, stores in a 5-minute in-memory map, and validates on callback." The actual OAuth CSRF protection is the unguessable `stateToken` GitHub echoes, so impact is limited, but a documented verification step that no code performs is a dead control that reads as covered; either wire it into `githubAuthCallback` or delete it and correct the risk table.

samples.summary: The nonce reaches the browser through `open(url)`, exposing it via argv to other local users on Linux
samples.evidence: `await open(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:79-80) passes the URL — nonce included — as an argv entry of the spawned handler, readable from `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` by any other local user under the default `hidepid=0`. A local attacker who reads the nonce can then send `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<their code>&state=<nonce>`, which passes `stateMatches` (login.ts:276) and is exchanged and saved as the user's session. The change acknowledges this in-code (login.ts:47-57) and in docs/design/rest-api.md:379 as an open item requiring a PKCE-shaped `/auth/cli/start`; recording it here so the residual gap is not lost — the nonce is a binding value, not a secret, and should not be relied on as one.

samples.summary: A detected injection attempt (wrong nonce) is silent to the user — no stderr warning, only an eventual timeout
samples.evidence: The wrong-nonce branch answers `400 State mismatch` to the requester and returns without touching the terminal (login.ts:276-280). A user under active authorization-code injection therefore sees nothing but "Login timed out. Try again with `wafflebase login`" 30 seconds later, and has no signal that something on their machine or in their browser is spraying codes at the loopback port. Emitting a `console.error` on each rejected callback would make the one security event this control is designed to detect visible.
searchedFor: grep for console.error/console.warn inside startCallbackServer in packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts
read of the full request handler (login.ts:240-325)
grep for a logger/telemetry module used by the CLI login path

samples.summary: The loopback callback server never checks `req.method`, contradicting the design doc's "accepts only GET"
samples.evidence: docs/design/cli.md:190-191 (in the paragraph this change rewrites) states "The local server binds to `127.0.0.1` only, accepts only `GET /callback`". The handler created at login.ts:240 checks only `url.pathname`; `req.method` is never inspected, so a cross-origin form POST (or any other method) to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…&state=…` is handled identically. The nonce now carries the real protection so exploitability is low, but a stated restriction that nothing enforces is a gate that reads as covered; add `if (req.method !== 'GET')` or correct the doc.
searchedFor: read of the full createServer handler in packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:240-325

samples.summary: `normalizeCliState` runs only inside the valid-port branch, so a malformed `cliState` with an out-of-range port is silently ignored rather than rejected
samples.evidence: github-auth.guard.ts:67-78 nests the `normalizeCliState(cliState)` call inside `if (Number.isInteger(portNum) && portNum >= 1024 && portNum <= 65535)`. With `?mode=cli&port=80&cliState=<garbage>` no validation runs, no state token is created, and the request falls through to the plain web flow (cookies set, redirect to FRONTEND_URL at auth.controller.ts:146-149) — exactly the "silent drop" outcome the function's own doc comment says must never happen. Hoisting the `normalizeCliState` call above the port check would make the validation uniform for every `mode=cli` request.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. login.ts:263-271 settles the login promise with callbackReject on a callback that carries no `state`, in contrast to the wrong-nonce branch at login.ts:276-280 which returns 400 without settling so the real callback can still win. The handler (login.ts:240-281) performs no Origin/Host/Referer/Sec-Fetch validation, so any local process or a cross-origin browser page issuing a no-cors GET to http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=X (port guessable by scanning within the 30s window, login.ts:327-335) can abort any in-flight login. The rejection text (login.ts:216-220) asserts a cause the CLI cannot distinguish and advertises `--allow-unbound-callback`; that flag (login.ts:17-21, 24, 62) sets options.allowUnbound, which skips the `received === null` guard so a nonce-less injected code is accepted — confirmed by test/login-callback.test.ts:103-112 — and is then exchanged at login.ts:92-102 and persisted as the user's session at login.ts:170-180. That is an auth downgrade squarely in the security lane (weakened binding/nonce check plus attacker-triggerable denial of the auth flow). No guard elsewhere makes the branch unreachable, so there is no ground to refute.

finding.evidence: login.ts:71-76 builds `oauthUrl` with `&cliState=<nonce>` but prints `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}` — deliberately nonce-stripped — and the old "If the browser does not open, visit the URL above." line was removed; the full URL is printed only in the `catch` around `open()`. `open()` frequently resolves successfully while opening nothing (SSH sessions with a stub xdg-open, WSL, containers), and docs/design/cli.md:176 still documents step 3 as "(also prints URL for copy-paste in headless environments)". A user who copies the printed URL starts a flow with no `cliState`, so `normalizeCliState` returns undefined (github-auth.guard.ts:70), `state.cliState` is falsy at auth.controller.ts:130, and the loopback redirect carries no `state`. The CLI then aborts with UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE, which blames the server and recommends `--allow-unbound-callback` — training the ordinary headless user to run every login with the anti-injection binding disabled. verdict.reason: Verified in the repo. login.ts:71-73 builds oauthUrl WITH `&cliState=<nonce>`, but the unconditional print at login.ts:74-76 emits only `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}` — nonce stripped; the full URL is printed only inside the `catch` around `open()` (login.ts:81-87), so an `open()` that resolves without launching a browser (SSH stub xdg-open, WSL, container) leaves the stripped line as the only affordance. Copying it produces a flow with no cliState: normalizeCliState(undefined) returns undefined (github-auth.guard.ts:25-28) and is passed to createState (guard:70-75); auth.controller.ts:130-132 then finds `state.cliState` falsy and redirects to the loopback with no `state` (controller:133-135). The CLI rejects that at login.ts:263-271 with UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE (login.ts:216-220), which misattributes the cause to an outdated server and recommends `--allow-unbound-callback` — the flag that disables the loopback callback binding whose purpose (login.ts:39-45) is to stop a locally injected authorization code from becoming this machine's session. docs/design/cli.md:176 and :1177 still document the printed URL as the headless copy-paste path, so this is the documented flow. Security-relevant under this lens: the sole recovery path offered to ordinary headless users trains them to run login with the anti-injection nonce check turned off, i.e. an auth control routinely moved out of the enforced path. No guard elsewhere restores the nonce to the printed line, so no refutation ground (not-present / already-guarded / out-of-scope) applies.

finding.summary: The anti-injection nonce is not secret from the very attacker it targets — it is handed to the browser via argv and printed to stderr
finding.evidence: The whole defence added here rests on `state` (login.ts:40) being unguessable by "another local process" (comment login.ts:33-39, docs/design/cli.md, rest-api.md risk table). But the nonce is embedded in `oauthUrl` (login.ts:44-46), which is (a) printed with `console.error` (login.ts:47) and (b) passed to `open(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:52), which spawns the browser/xdg-open with the full URL as a command-line argument. On Linux/macOS with default settings any local process — including one running as a different unprivileged user — can read that argv (`/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `ps auxww`). Attack: local attacker polls `ps` during `wafflebase login`, reads `cliState=<nonce>` and `port=<port>`, then starts their own flow `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim port>&cliState=<stolen nonce>` authenticating as the ATTACKER's GitHub account. The backend mints a code for the attacker's user and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=…&state=<stolen nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:130-135); `stateMatches` (login.ts:210) passes, the victim's CLI exchanges the attacker's code and saves the attacker's tokens as the session — the exact code-injection/session-fixation this change claims to close. A value-echo nonce cannot fix this because the value the CLI expects is the value it leaks; the standard fix is PKCE (CLI sends `code_challenge` in the URL, keeps the verifier in-process, and `POST /auth/cli/exchange` requires the verifier so a code minted for another challenge cannot be redeemed).

verdict.reason: The core mechanism is present and the attack chain is reachable. login.ts:80 passes the nonce-bearing oauthUrl to open(), exposing the 32-byte cliState in child-process argv (/proc/<pid>/cmdline, ps). github-auth.guard.ts:67-77 accepts an arbitrary attacker-supplied port and a merely format-validated cliState (normalizeCliState, guard:25-41), and auth.controller.ts:126-135 mints a code for whoever completed OAuth and redirects it to 127.0.0.1:<attacker-chosen port>?code=...&state=<supplied nonce>. The victim listener's sole binding is the value-echo comparison (login.ts:276, stateMatches login.ts:200-208), which the stolen nonce satisfies, and POST /auth/cli/exchange (auth.controller.ts:152-168) requires no verifier, so the attacker's code becomes the victim's session - the exact injection/session-fixation the nonce claims to close. No PKCE/code_verifier exists in the backend, and no guard blocks the path; the repo itself records this as an unmitigated "Open" risk (docs/design/rest-api.md:379, docs/design/cli.md:205-218), which is documentation, not a guard. One sub-claim of the evidence is inaccurate - the nonce is NOT printed on the normal path; login.ts:74-76 prints a deliberately nonce-free URL and only the open()-failure fallback (login.ts:86) prints the full URL - but that does not remove the argv vector, so it is not a basis to refute.
